1
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici Curiae States of Florida, Georgia, Kansas,
Louisiana, Nebraska, and Oklahoma  routinely bring
criminal forfeiture actions to remove from criminal
hands the tools of criminal enterprise.  Forfeiture protects citizens by depriving offenders of the means to
repeat their crimes.  Because it aims to remove  the
instrumentalities of crimes, forfeiture uniquely makes
it harder for criminals  to continue violating state
laws.
This case bears directly on Amici States’ ability to
use forfeiture to protect their citizens.   Jouppi’s position, if adopted, would require  states to expend more
resources and clear unnecessarily high hurdles when
seeking to establish a forfeiture’s proportionality.  But
neither the Constitution’s text nor historical forfeiture
practice nor this Court’s precedents impose such a
hurdle.  And for good reasons.  Amici therefore respectfully ask this Court to affirm.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Kenneth Jouppi’s fine was not excessive.  He used
his plane to transport alcohol bound for an Alaska village that had chosen to prohibit it, and in doing so
subjected his plane to forfeiture.  Pet. App. 3a–5a.  Under the Excessive Fines Clause, the question is
whether that forfeiture was “grossly disproportional
to the gravity of [his] offense.”  United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321, 334 (1998).  Jouppi argues that
courts must assess his “own wrongdoing” rather than
evaluate the offense “purely in the abstract.”  Pet. Br.
13.  That’s a false choice.

2
The Court’s cases already require some abstraction—identifying the kind of harm the forfeiture statute targets  and considering  the potential harm an
offender could cause.  The Alaska Supreme Court followed binding precedent and correctly used the appropriate level of abstraction to answer those questions.
And the plane’s direct role in the offense makes it a
classic instrumentality of the crime, suggest ing that
its forfeiture was presumptively proportional.
For decades, alcohol abuse has scourged Alaskan
communities.  For example, as of 2025, “3,000 American Indian or Alaska Native” minors aged 12 to 17 suffered from alcohol use disorder. 1  For adults 18 and
older, that number is 130,000. 2  To further quantify
the harms of alcohol, consider that in Alaska roughly
562 people die each year due to excessive alcohol use.3
And around the time of Jouppi’s crime, excessive alcohol consumption cost Alaska approximately $900 million.4
To address this crisis, t he Alaska legislature allows communities within the state to ban the importation or possession of alcohol.   Alaska Stat.


1 Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) in the United States: Age Groups
and Demographic Characteristics, Nat’l Inst. on Alcohol Abuse &
Alcoholism, https://perma.cc/S8EV-GSEZ (last updated Aug.
2025).
2 Id.
3 Alcohol Abuse Statistics , Nat’l Ctr. for Drug Abuse Stat.,
https://perma.cc/GCC7-NUHN (last visited Oct. 7, 2026).
4  Id.

3
§ 04.11.491(a)(5) (2025).  Indeed, the legislature originally passed this law in response to reports and studies revealing that excessive alcohol consumption,
especially in rural communities, significantly contributed to crime across the state.  Pet. App. 20a–21a.
The communities that ban the importation or possession of alcohol , known as “dry villages,” are often
in remote areas with limited medical and law-enforcement resources.  One such village is Beaver, Alaska,
where fewer than 100 people live.  Beaver has banned
possessing, selling, and importing alcohol.
At the time of the crime,  Jouppi operated an airtaxi company.  Pet. App. 3a–4a.  He was preparing to
fly a passenger to Beaver when Alaska State Troopers
observed him loading his passenger’s cargo onto his
plane.  Pet. App. 32a–33a.  Just before takeoff, troopers stopped him and found nine gallons of beer on the
plane.  Pet. App. 33a.
Jouppi and his company were charged with misdemeanor importation.  Pet. App. 33a.  At trial, troopers
testified that at least one six-pack of beer was in plain
view, but Jouppi testified that he was unaware of any
alcohol on the plane .  Pet. App. 4a, 153a–54a.  The
jury ultimately found him guilty, determining that he
either knew about or was deliberately ignorant of the
alcohol.  Pet. App. 5a.
During sentencing, the state trial court found that
Jouppi was “willfully blind” as to the visible six-pack.
Pet. App. 7a.  It therefore sentenced him to 180 days
(177 suspended) and a $3,000 fine ($1,500 suspended).
Pet. App. 5a .  As to the plane, t he trial court ultimately decided against forfeiture.  Pet. App. 6a.  But

4
the Alaska Supreme Court disagreed, concluding that
Jouppi’s fine (including forfeiture of the plane) was
not excessive.  Pet. App. 29a.  Jouppi petitioned for a
writ of certiorari, which this Court granted.
The Court should affirm.  Under United States v.
Bajakajian, “a punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is grossly disproportional to the
gravity of a defendant’s offense.”  524 U.S. at 334.
Two considerations support the Alaska Supreme
Court’s conclusion that forfeiture of Jouppi’s plane
satisfies that standard.
First, Jouppi’s insistence that a court may focus
only on his “own wrongdoing” is incomplete .  To
properly assess whether a fine is excessive, a  court
must distill the essential features of a criminal’s
wrongdoing to determine whether the offender belongs to the class the statute principally targets.  It
must also assess the potential harm of his conduct :
what might have happened had the crime gone undetected, and whether that potential ha rm matches the
danger the statute addresses.  The Alaska Supreme
Court rightfully did both.  It matched the potential
harm of Jouppi’s own wrongdoing—smuggling alcohol
into a dry village —to the danger Alaska ’s dry-village
law targets.
Second, property forfeiture is presumptively proportional when the forfeited property was an instrumentality of the crime.  Our history strongly supports
this presumption.  The Court should give that history
effect when applying the gross -disproportionality
standard.

5
Because the Alaska Supreme Court’s decision respected both those principles, the Court should affirm.
ARGUMENT
I. The Alaska Supreme Court did not evaluate
Jouppi’s conduct “purely in the abstract.”
The Eighth Amendment prohibits imposing “excessive fines.”  Forfeitures are “‘fines’ if they constitute punishment for an offense.”  Bajakajian, 524 U.S.
at 328.  And “a punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is grossly disproportional to the
gravity of a defendant’s offense.”  Id. at 334.
Jouppi’s fine was not excessive.  The court properly
considered the kind of conduct he committed and the
harm it could cause.  He argues that courts must evaluate an offense “not purely in the abstract, but with
reference to the defendant’s own wrongdoing. ”  Pet.
Br. 13.  That focus still requires identifying the class
of wrongdoing and assessing potential harm —both
abstract inquiries that use the offender’s conduct as a
reference point.  And those inquiries operate under a
deferential gross-disproportionality standard, not a
demand for precisely calibrated punishment.  The
Alaska Supreme Court followed that approach.  And
Jouppi’s historical examples and objections to the decision below do not establish otherwise.
A. The Court’s cases ask the abstract question of whether the offender belongs to
the group the statute targets.
To Jouppi, courts must make a binomial choice between evaluating harm with reference to specific
wrongdoing or pure abstraction.  Pet. Br. i.  Yet the

6
alternatives are not so finely distinct.  Controlling authority from this Court  demands some abstraction.
Bajakajian asked whether an offender belonged to
“the class of persons for whom the statute was principally designed.”  524 U.S. at 338.  That question requires a court to distill the essential features of the
offender’s own wrongdoing and compare them with
the conduct the statute principally targets.   The offender’s specific circumstances form a reference point,
but his criminal conduct must then be situated within
the broader class of persons the statute seeks to regulate.  In this case —those who traffic alcohol into
Alaska’s dry villages.
Statutes necessarily group different acts by shared
features.  Bajakajian, for its part, involved a statute
targeting the “money launderer,” “drug trafficker,” or
“tax evader.”  Id.  An offender’s circumstances will differ, but a court identifies the kind of wrongdoing that
places them within (or without) the class.  And even
among those who commit the same category of wrongdoing, the offenders will have varying degree s of culpability.  The currency -reporting statute in
Bajakajian covered those who failed to report $10,001
in currency alongside those who failed to report
$1,000,000.  See id. at 324–25.  Alaska’s alcohol-smuggling statute similarly covers different quantities of
alcohol.  But determining the shared features the statute targets necessarily requires some abstraction.
Other features of the gross -disproportionality test
also require abstraction.  The Constitution doesn’t require strict proportionality or a unique punishment
for every imaginable offense variation.  Because of
that inherent variability, Bajakajian emphasized two

7
important principles.  First, “judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first
instance to the legislature.”  Id. at 336.  Second, “any
judicial determination regarding the gravity of a particular criminal offense will be inherently imprecise.”
Id.  Courts therefore owe substantial deference to the
legislature’s judgment, even when reasonable minds
may disagree about the appropriate punishment.  See
id.  Both principles focus on abstract questions rather
than the defendant’s own wrongdoing.  Jouppi, for his
part, all but acknowledges this by demanding only
that a court consider wrongdoing “not purely in the
abstract.”  Pet. Br. 13 (emphasis added).
B. Courts must engage in abstraction to outline the potential harm of an offender’s
conduct.
Identifying the group the statute targets  solves
one-half of the equation.  A court must also consider
“the gravity of the defendant’s offense. ”  Bajakajian,
524 U.S. at 337.  But that too requires some abstraction.  The gravity of an offender’s own wrongdoing includes its potential harm.  Courts can assess gravity
by “measuring the harm caused or threatened.”  Solem v. Helm , 463 U.S. 277, 292 –93 (1983).  That requires asking what might have happened had the
conduct gone undetected, using its essential features
to identify the possible consequences.  The inquiry begins with  the offender’s wrongdoing as a reference
point, but then considers the harms that could have
followed.  Again, that necessarily requires some abstraction.

8
No one could doubt the harms associated with alcohol abuse.  At the national level, almost 500 Americans die each day because of excessive alcohol use. 5
And almost 10% of Americans aged 12 and older suffer
from Alcohol Use Disorder.6  Alaska tragically has the
third-highest rate of all states for alcohol -related
deaths per 10,000 adults, with a rate of 10.15. 7  This
correlates to an average 562 annual deaths caused by
excessive alcohol use. 8  And i n 2018, the estimated
cost of alcohol misuse in Alaska was $2.4 billion.9
The Alaskan legislature justified the statute based
on those harms, but those harms obviously do not
arise every time someone imports alcohol.  Potential
harm requires considering a chain of events that may
or may not follow from the offender’s own wrongdoing.
If alcohol reaches a dry village, generally someone
must consume it before its effects can contribute to injury, crime, or other harm.  A court cannot know
which consequence will follow in a particular case.  It
can, however, identify the potential harm of the prohibited transportation and determine  whether that


5 Alcohol Abuse Statistics , Nat’l Ctr. for Drug Abuse Stat. ,
https://perma.cc/GCC7-NUHN (last visited Oct. 7, 2026).
6 Id.
7 Id.  Only New Mexico and Wyoming have higher rates, with
12.86 and 10.23, respectively.
8 Id.
9 McDowell Grp., The Economic Costs of Alcohol Misuse in
Alaska: 2019 Update  1 (2020).  This cost includes those associated with productivity loss, traffic collisions, criminal justice,
public assistance, and health care.  Id.

9
harm matches the danger the statute targets.  Uncertainty about the precise outcome makes the inquiry
hypothetical; it does not, however, make it guesswork.
Nor does it mark some arbitrary judicial departure
from analyzing an offender’s own wrongdoing.
Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U.S. 263 (1980), illustrates
the point.  Rummel involved a financial crime, and the
Court observed that if the defendant “attempted to defraud his victim of $50,000, but had failed, no money
whatsoever would have changed hands; yet [he] would
be no less blameworthy, only less skillful, than if he
had succeeded.”  Id. at 276.  That assessment relied
on a hypothetical loss, not the consummated fraud
(which never happened).  Potential harm belonged in
the assessment because it is a logical consequence of
the defendant’s wrongdoing.
The plane forfeiture  doesn’t become  excessive
merely because Jouppi was “less skillful”  and got
caught before his crime caused its reasonably foreseeable harms.   Id.  The happenstance of being apprehended doesn’t diminish culpability.
The Alaska Supreme Court did nothing more in its
analysis of Jouppi’s crime.
C. The gross -disproportionality test is extremely deferential.
For defendants, t he gross -disproportionality
standard is demanding by design.  Bajakajian
“adopt[ed] the standard of gross disproportionality articulated in our Cruel and Unusual Punishments
Clause precedents.”  Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336.
Jouppi co ncedes that the standard is so demanding
that “the Court has long fractured over whether any

10
proportionality limit obtains at all,” in those cases.
Pet. Br. 15 (citing  Harmelin v. Michigan , 501 U.S.
957, 966–85 (1991) and Ewing v. California, 538 U.S.
11, 32 (2003) (Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment)).
Consider, for example, the punishment scheme in
Ewing, which permitted the same sentence for murder
and a recidivist who stole three golf clubs.  538 U.S. at
28 (plurality opinion) .  There, the Supreme Court
acknowledged Ewing’s sentence was “a long one,”
“[b]ut it reflects a rational legislative judgment, entitled to deference, that offenders who have committed
serious or violent felonies and who continue to commit
felonies must be incapacitated.”  Id. at 30.
Yet Jouppi’s theory would subject fines to far
greater constitutional exactions than the punishment
this Court blessed in Ewing—life imprisonment for
golf club theft.   In reality, Jouppi’s proportionality
concerns pale in comparison.  To be sure, Jouppi considers the forfeiture  of his plane “excessive.”  But
Ewing, no doubt, thought a lifetime of imprisonment
was an excessive price to pay for stealing three golf
clubs from a pro shop.  The forfeiture statute here, in
Jouppi’s view, is “capaciously broad” and casts “an extraordinarily wide net” because a plane is subject to
forfeiture whether the pilot was smuggling one tall
boy or three barrels of beer.  Pet. Br. 38 (cleaned up).
And, he argues, a pilot can forfeit his plane for transporting a six-pack, but an automobile’s driver only forfeits his car if he carries more than 12 gallons of beer.
See Alaska Stat. § 04.16.220(i) (2025).
But this is Alaska, where many communities are
only reachable by plane .  And Alaska’s legislature —

11
no less than the one in Ewing—made “a rational legislative judgment, entitled to deference ,” that pilots
transporting alcohol by plane to remote, dry villages
represent an acute danger to Alaskans’ well -being.
Ewing, 538 U.S. at 30.
Jouppi’s plane-automobile comparisons in the statute fall far short of showing gross disproportionality.
The Cruel and Unusual Punishments cases illustrate
the magnitude of the required showing:  The proportionality principle would apply to the “extreme example” of making “overtime parking a felony punishable
by life imprisonment.”  Id. at 21 (quoting Rummel v.
Estelle, 445 U.S. 263, 274 n.11 (1980)).  Jouppi’s
claims simply are not on that same level.
D. The Alaska Supreme Court correctly applied the gross-disproportionality test.
Given that some abstraction is required, Jouppi ’s
version of the question presented is a false choice.  The
better question is:  How much abstraction is too much?
A closer look at Jouppi’s argument reveals that his
criticisms apply only when a court evaluat es wrongdoing at what he terms “the highest possible level of
generality.”  Pet. Br. 12.  By that, he seems to mean
what would be the extreme, worst-case scenario that
could arise if everyone broke the law in question.  Yet
that’s not what the Alaska Supreme Court did here,
so Jouppi’s criticism accomplishes little.
1. Jouppi’s historical examples are inapt.
Jouppi offers historical examples of courts leaning
into the worst-case scenario to justify a harsh punishment, see Pet. Br. at 22–32, but those examples only

12
vindicate the Alaska Supreme Court’s far more nuanced analysis.
Take the case of Henry Sherfield, who broke a pane
of a church’s stained-glass window.  The lords in the
Star Chamber invoked the consequences that would
result if no one  had to obey the church’s authority:
“[A]n insurrection may come of it.”   Pet. Br. 23 –24
(quoting Proceedings in the Star -Chamber against
Henry Sherfield (1632) in 3 T.B. Howell, State Trials
538 (1816)).
Or take the punishment of William Prynn, who authored a critique of stage plays despite knowing the
queen favored them.  Pet. Br. 24–25.  The lords again
feared that i f no one had to obey the crown’s dictate,
“Mr. Prynn would have a new government.”  Pet. Br.
25 (quoting Proceedings against Wm. Prynn, esq. in
the Star-Chamber (1632) in 3 T.B. Howell, State Trials 575 (1816)).
Consider yet another.  Lord Devonshire battered a
Colonel in the king’s palace.  If everyone behaved that
way in the palace, it would be akin to “pulling the king
out of his throne. ”  Pet. Br. 27 (quoting The Case of
William Earl of Devonshire (1687) in 11 T.B. Howell,
State Trials 1366 (1816)).
Jouppi’s examples from history show that only
these extreme justifications done at the highest level
of generality make a fine excessive.  That’s no surprise
given what the cases examining gross disproportionality have said.  See Ewing, 538 U.S. at 21.

13
2. The Alaska Supreme Court did not justify the
forfeiture at the highest level of generality.
But that is not what happened here.  The legislature identified a particular kind of wrongdoing —
bringing alcohol into a community that has chosen to
exclude it —in light of the dangers that community
has identifie d concerning alcohol.  Alaska Stat.
§ 04.11.491(a)(5) (2025).  Jouppi violated the law, and
Alaska’s approach doesn’t resemble a tyrannical authority justifying any punishment at stratospheric
levels of generality.
Jouppi first argues that the Alaska Supreme Court
deviated from analyzing his “own wrongdoing” and instead considered his offense “purely in the abstract,”
when it found that he “was ‘clearly within the class of
persons targeted by the statute.’”  Pet. Br. 38 (quoting
Pet. App. 20a).  But Bajakajian asked courts to identify the features of the targeted class and consider if
an offender’s wrongdoing matches .  See Bajakajian,
524 U.S. at 336–38.  And although the answer to Bajakajian’s question tends to suggest Jouppi’s fine was
not excessive, he counters that the Court could have
said the same thing in Bajakajian:  The statute at issue “applied to Hosep Bajakajian too.”  Pet. Br. 38.
Nonsense.  Bajakajian did not ask merely whether
the statute applied to the defendant.  It asked whether
he belonged to “the class of persons for whom the statute was principally designed .”  Bajakajian, 524 U.S.
at 338.  And the answer was no:  His reporting violation did not situate him alongside a “money launderer,” “drug trafficker,” or “tax evader.”  Id.

14
Here, Alaska targets a narrow group, one to which
Jouppi belongs.  The law applies to those who use “aircraft, vehicles, or vessels” to transport alcoholic beverages into dry villages.  Alaska Stat.
§ 04.16.220(a)(3) (2025).
Jouppi admits he violated the statute, but protests
that “the airplane -forfeiture provisio n applies with
undifferentiated force ‘to all.’”  Pet.  Br. 38  (citation
omitted).  I f by “all” Jouppi means “all pilots smuggling alcohol into dry villages in Alaska,” he’s right.
But that’s hardly the “expansive statute” Jouppi
makes it.  Pet. Br. 39.  The Alaska Supreme Court did
exactly what it was supposed to do:  It identified a reasonably sized class of people the statute targeted and
determined that Jouppi belonged in it.
Jouppi protests that  the Alaska Supreme Court
committed its next error of pure abstraction when it
deemed him culpable for “the harm . . . addressed in
the legislative history of the forfeiture provision,” and,
consequently, for all “the social ills of alcohol abuse
statewide.”  Pet. Br. 39.  Of course, nearly every criminal convicted of nearly every offense could lodge the
same complaint.
But even so, the Alaska Supreme Court did no such
thing.  Like the Court in Bajakajian, it identified the
harms at which the statute was aimed—“crime,” “disorders,” “[medical] conditions,” “death,” and “substantial costs” relating to “public health and the
administration of justice.”  Pet. App. 24a.  The legislative history made the targeted harm s apparent, and,
again, “Jouppi [was] plainly within the class of offenders it targeted.”  Id. at 25a n.94.  It did not “saddle[]
Jouppi with the social ills of alcohol abuse statewide.”

15
Pet. Br. 39.  Rather, Jouppi’s wrongdoing matched the
statute’s target.  He loaded alcohol onto an aircraft
bound for Beaver, a village that had chosen to prohibit
alcohol.
As the above establishes, a court for forfeiture purposes need not myopically focus on the defendant’s
own wrongdoing .  Indeed, this Court requires precisely what the Alaska Supreme Court did:  consider
the somewhat abstract questions of what harm the
statute targets, and whether the essential features of
a defendant’s wrongdoing match that targeted harm.
Even if it is error for a court to consider wrongdoing
at the highest possible level of generality, that didn’t
happen here.  If Bajakajian is an example of Jouppi’s
preferred “standard in practice,” Pet. Br. 16, then he
has no basis for criticizing the Alaska Supreme
Court’s decision.
II. The plan e was an instrumentality of the
crime, which  supports the holding  that the
forfeiture was not grossly disproportionate.
Our nation’s established history of forfeiting offending property —instrumentalities of the crime —
supports that holding.  The Court’s modern cases do
not prohibit considering the property’s connection to
the offense.  Here, the plane was the means Jouppi
used for the prohibited transport.  The Court should
affirm and recognize that forfeiture of a classic instrumentality is presumptively proportional.

16
A. Instrumentality forfeitures have a long
and storied history.
Since the founding, our law  has allowed governments to seek forfeiture of property used as instrumentalities of crimes.  The property itself, being used
to perpetrate a crime, was considered to have committed the offense.  See Austin v. United States, 509 U.S.
602, 624–25 (1993) (Scalia, J., concurring in part and
concurring in the judgment).   “English Law
provid[ing] for statutory forfeitures of offending objects used in violation of the customs and revenue
laws” reflects this theory that property can be tainted
by crime.  Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht Leasing Co.,
416 U.S. 663, 682 (1974).  And the Colonies, “before
the adoption of the Constitution,” enforced this type of
English forfeiture  against commodities and vessels .
Id. at 683; see also C.J. Hendry Co. v. Moore, 318 U.S.
133, 139, 140 n.4, 143 (1943).  Indeed, even after adoption of the Excessive Fines Clause , American courts
commonly ordered and upheld forfeiture of vessels
used to violate the law.
Remarkably salient is one early example.  In Phile
v. The Ship Anna , 1 U.S. (1 Dall.) 197 (Pa. Ct. Com.
Pl. 1787), a vessel had transported “forty two hampers
of porter . . . with out being first duly entered at the
Collector’s office.”  Id. at 197.  The ship’s manifest had
declared only twenty hampers.  Id. at 205.  The judge
explained that this was not “a hard nor a novel case,”
and that “[i]f the Legislature has thought proper to
subject the owners to this forfeiture, we must submit.”
Id. at 207.  The jury then found in favor of forfeiture.
Id. at 208.

17
Later cases continued to follow this approach.  A
1799 revenue act required vessels to have permits to
dock in American ports  if carrying foreign goods exceeding $400 in value .  See The Harmony, 11 F. Cas.
556, 557 (C.C.D. Mass. 1812)  (No. 6081).  Under this
statute, Justice Story, while riding circuit, upheld the
forfeiture of a vessel docked in Boston that had received foreign goods from a British ship  while in
American waters.  Id. at 557–59.
Early Congresses , when  prohibiting the African
slave trade , decided that vessels used in the trade
should be forfeited.  Cf. The St. Jago de Cuba, 22 U.S.
(9 Wheat.) 409, 409 –14 (1824); The Catharine, 25 F.
Cas. 332, 338 (C.C.D.N.Y. 1840)  (No. 14,755) .  And
courts routinely upheld forfeiture of  the vessels even
when they did not arrive in Africa or pick up slaves .
See The Catharine, 25 F. Cas . at 341.  In The Catharine, for instance, the court ordered forfeiture upon a
showing that the vessel had set sail for Africa with the
purpose of transporting slaves.  Id. at 339–41.
Forfeiture of vessels importing alcohol into Alaska
has also been part of this long, historical use of forfeiture.  Soon after the United States purchased Alaska,
Congress passed an act governing “customs, commerce, and navigation” in the territory, and the President, pursuant to the act, promulgated an executive
order prohibiting the importa tion of “distilled spirits
into or within the territory of Alaska.”  See The Louisa
Simpson, 15 F. Cas. 953, 954 (D. Or. 1871) (No. 8533).
In 1870, a vessel docked at an Alaskan port traded alcohol and other goods to the residents there.  Id. at
957.  A trial court upheld forfeiture of the vessel  and
her cargo.  Id. at 958.

18
Forfeiture for alcohol-related offenses extended beyond ships.  In Dobbins’s Distillery v. United States ,
96 U.S. 395 , 396 –97 (1877), the owner of property
leased it to a company that, without the owner’s
knowledge, operated a distillery and intended to conceal its revenue .  An act of Congress “attache[d] the
offence to the distillery” and further provided that
“the distillery  . . . shall be forfeited to the United
States.”  Id. at 400–01.
These early cases establis h important principles.
Forfeiting a vessel smuggling alcohol was an ordinary
and expected feature of the law.  See The Ship Anna,
1 U.S. at 207  (“[I]n England it has long existed, and
before the revolution it was known in Pennsylvania.”).
It didn’t matter whether the vessel reached its destination.  The Catharine, 25 F. Cas. at 339 –41.  And
such forfeiture practices continued  after the Fourteenth Amendment’s passage in cases with facts similar to those here.  See The Louisa Simpson, 15 F. Cas.
at 957–58.  These principles were not limited to ships.
See Dobbins’s Distillery, 96 U.S. at 400–401.
B. The Court should consider that Jouppi’s
plane was an instrumentality of his crime.
The Court’s decisions in Austin and Bajakajian do
not require it to disregard the relationship of an instrumentality and the offense.   First, in Austin the
Court found that “civil in rem forfeitures are fines for
purposes of the Eighth Amendment when they are at
least partially punitive.”  Timbs v. Indiana, 586 U.S.
146, 155  (2019).  Second, in Bajakajian, the Court
found that “a punitive forfeiture  violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is grossly disproportional to the
gravity of a defendant’s offense.”  524 U.S. at 334.

19
If most in rem forfeitures and all punitive forfeitures apply the gross-disproportionality test, what is
left of the historic instrumentality test?  The Court
has never “rule[d] out the possibility that the connection between the property and the offense may be relevant . . . in determining whether the forfeiture  . . .
[is] excessive.”  Austin, 509 U.S. at 623 n.15.  The
Court has cautioned not to rely on the “technical distinction between proceedings in rem and proceedings
in personam.”  Austin, 509 U.S. at 615 n.9.  And a government may “effectively merg[e] the in rem forfeiture
proceeding with the in personam criminal proceeding”
where the statute “maintains traditional in rem forfeiture’s focus on tainted property.”  Honeycutt v.
United States, 581 U.S. 443, 453 (2017).
Answering the question presented in Jouppi’s favor, however,  might close the door that Austin left
open and leave centuries of our legal tradition behind.
Jouppi’s forfeiture here has the hallmarks of a civil in
rem forfeiture.  It fits squarely into the “guilty property” category  as an instrumentality of the crime .
That is because  “instrumentality” “fairly characterizes property that historically was subject to forfeiture
because it was the actual means by which an offense
was committed.”  Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 333 n.8
(cleaned up).  And “[i]nstrumentality forfeitures have
historically been limited to the property actually used
to commit an offense and no more.”  Id.
Alaska’s forfeiture statute applies only to property
used to commit the crime.  Under the statute, “aircraft, vehicles, or vessels used to transport or facilitate the transportation of . . . alcoholic beverages
imported into a municipality or established village in

20
violation of [the dry -village statute]” “are subject to
forfeiture.”  Alaska Stat. §  04.16.220(a), (a)(3),
(a)(3)(C) (2025).  The statute is consistent with
Alaska’s general move away from civil forfeiture.  See
Alaska Stat. § 09.55.700 (2025) (“in rem forfeiture actions are abolished if used instead of a criminal proceeding”).  And the airplane at issue here was “the
actual means by which an offense was committed .”
Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 333 n.8.  It was the very plane
Jouppi was going to fly to Beaver with alcohol, before
troopers stopped him.
The Court should hold that when, as here, the forfeiture involves a classic instrumentality of the crime,
the forfeiture should be viewed as presumptively proportional.  The traditional inquiry would not entail
“determining the appropriate value of the penalty in
relation to the committed offense, but by determining
what property has been ‘tainted’ by unlawful use.”
Austin, 509 U.S. at 627 (Scalia, J., concurring in part).
After all, “[s]cales used to measure out unlawful drug
sales, for example, are confiscable whether made of
the purest gold or the basest metal. ”  Id.  Bajakajian
doesn’t preclude this approach because  there, “[t]he
currency in question [was] not an instrumentality ,”
but merely “ the subject of the crime of failure to report.”  Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 334 n.9.  Jouppi’s plane
was the means of the crime.  That direct relationship,
reinforced by the historical treatment of vessels used
for unlawful transport, supports a presumption of proportionality.
CONCLUSION
The Court should affirm the decision of the Alaska
Supreme Court.
